9.0.0.en: About a week after Christ's earlier talk about His sufferings, His death and His resurrection, and about His Kingdom coming with power, He took with Him three of His disciples, who enjoyed more love and faith than the others, and went up with them onto a high mountain. There His appearance (form) was changed before them, and He appeared in great glory, as we shall see. But the following meanings concern us here:

9.0.1.en: (1) Only three disciples: with God there is no partiality, but the one who is better prepared receives greater blessings. (2) A high mountain: no one can behold the glories of God unless he rises up and the world grows small before his eyes.

9.1.0.en: St. Mark here describes the manner of this change in the Lord's appearance, for His garments became exceedingly white, shining like light or radiance. To show the intensity of the brightness, he added that no fuller on earth can whiten them so. The fuller is the one who whitens cloth, as the last step in the making of spun and woven fabric.

9.2.0.en: And together with the change of His appearance into this glory, Elijah appeared to them, who represents the prophets and the living (because he had not yet died), and represents virginity and its high degree (because he did not marry). Moses also appeared, who represents those who have fallen asleep in the hope of Christ's redemption, and also the spiritual leadership of the people of God. Both of them fasted forty days, as a symbol of the holiness in which they lived on earth, and also as a symbol of the form of the spiritual life, whether in monasticism or in the sacrament of marriage. And in honor of them, St. Mark added that they were talking with Jesus.

9.2.1.en: My beloved brother ... have we thought about obtaining the honor and blessings of talking with Jesus?!!

9.3.0.en: With the surprise, awesomeness and splendor of the sight, Peter spoke, declaring his happiness with this vision, and that heavenly spiritual feelings are better than earthly emotions however splendid they may be. But he also added, according to his human thinking, that Christ with Elijah and Moses might be in need of tabernacles to shelter them. St. Mark attributes this saying of Peter to the state of terror he was in during the transfiguration.

9.4.0.en: "A cloud that overshadowed them": St. Matthew added (Mt 17:5) that this cloud was "bright", to indicate the divine presence, just as the bright cloud appeared to Aaron (Ex 16:10) ... And the appearance of the cloud was accompanied by the Father's declaration concerning His Son and His divinity, exactly as happened at the Baptism of Christ.

9.5.0.en: And suddenly the heavenly scene ended, and the form of the Lord returned to its first nature, and Moses and Elijah disappeared. And as they came down, Christ charged them to tell no one what they had seen until after He had risen from the dead. Yet they did not understand at that time the meaning of His rising from the dead, but they did not ask Him about it; rather they kept everything to themselves (within them).

9.5.2.en: (1) Perhaps the disciples recognized the persons of Moses and Elijah either by the Spirit, or because Christ pronounced their names during the conversation.

9.5.3.en: 2) "(It is good for us to be here": a life of contemplation and retreat is good for the servant and the spiritual person, for he takes from it provision and strength that help him to go down to the field of service and suffering.

9.5.4.en: (3) Christ's conversation with Elijah and Moses shows that there is unceasing speech between God and His saints. Therefore the Church teaches us that, besides speaking with God, we can speak with the saints in our prayers (without worshiping them).

9.5.5.en: (4) If the sight was so splendid to this degree, how will the sight be in heaven, my friend?! Come ... take courage ... how beautiful is heaven with its Christ and its saints!! And do not forget that you have a place there.

9.6.0.en: The appearance of Elijah at the transfiguration raised a question among the disciples, which they put to Christ: the scribes teach the people that Elijah must appear first, before the appearance of Christ; and if what we have seen is what is meant, how can Elijah's appearance be after Christ?!

9.7.0.en: "Elijah indeed comes first": that is, what the scribes say is correct in this teaching, that Elijah precedes the appearance of Christ.

9.7.1.en: "And restores all things": that is, he brings the Jews back by repentance, in preparation for receiving Christ.

9.7.2.en: "That He must suffer many things and be set at nought": the disciples had a limited outlook, and so they did not understand that Christ must suffer (Isa; 53:2, Ps 22:6).

9.7.3.en: "Elijah ... is come": a clear reference to John the Baptist, who resembled Elijah in his work and in his person. John came and the Jews killed him (they did to him whatever they wished). See also the explanation of (Mt 17:10-13).

9.8.s.en: (3) The healing of a boy with an unclean spirit

9.8.0.en: "Greatly amazed, and running": St. Mark depicts the state of the crowd on seeing Christ, for they ran to Him out of their joy ... As for their amazement, it was because of His sudden absence and their not knowing where He was. After the transfiguration, the Lord Jesus returned with His three disciples to the rest of the disciples, and found many questioning them, among them the scribes, who seized the opportunity of the Teacher's absence to embarrass the disciples. Therefore, when Christ arrived, the first thing He said was a question to the scribes: "What question ye with them?" The purpose of His question was to relieve His disciples of the embarrassment and to answer on their behalf.

9.9.0.en: The Lord Christ received no answer from the scribes, for a man in great need interrupted the conversation, saying: I have brought unto Thee my son, which hath a dumb spirit, and I did not find You. And St. Luke adds that he was his father's only child (Lk 9:38). St. Mark mentioned this story here to show that our struggle with Satan continues, and that faith in Christ is necessary for victory over him to be achieved ... And the man began to explain the symptoms of Satan's dwelling in him and raging.

9.9.1.en: "Wheresoever he taketh him": when Satan rages against him.

9.9.2.en: "He teareth him": he subjects him to severe fits, so that he makes involuntary movements by which he harms himself.

9.9.3.en: "And he foameth, and gnasheth with his teeth": symptoms resembling epilepsy, so that the mouth convulses and the saliva flows, and all his muscles stiffen and he loses the ability to move ... "And I spake to thy disciples" - in Your absence - "that they should cast him out; and they could not."

9.10.0.en: The Lord Christ answered with a reply that carried a rebuke. But for whom was this rebuke?

9.10.2.en: First: the rebuke may be for the disciples, who, because of the weakness of their faith, were not able to cast out this devil and heal the sufferer.

9.10.3.en: Second: perhaps the blame is for the father who - despite his need - was doubtful, and his faith was not complete, for he said in his words to Christ: "If Thou canst do any thing?"

9.10.4.en: Third: the blame may be for the whole crowd, which had seen so many earlier miracles and did not believe, as shown by the Lord's saying: "O generation".

9.10.5.en: "How long shall I suffer you?": Of course Christ bore much, and will also bear, the weaknesses of His disciples, especially at His passion and crucifixion ... But what is meant here is to make clear that God's heart cannot bear unbelief in Him or doubt of Him, for this wounds Him greatly. Therefore He also rebuked the disciples for their little faith ... and in the incident of the sea raging against the boat (Mt 8:23-26), and also when He rebuked Peter when he doubted and began to sink (Mt 14:25-32).

9.10.6.en: "Bring him unto Me": proof of the Lord Jesus' tenderness toward us, and a confirmation of His saying in (Mt 11:28): "Come unto Me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

9.11.0.en: When the boy came near to Christ, Satan raged exceedingly, so that he cast the boy down cruelly, and he wallowed and foamed (his saliva flowed).

9.11.1.en: ... This teaches us Satan's cruelty and evil on the one hand, and also shows that he knew he was certainly going out. Therefore it is as though he were fighting in despair his last war...

9.12.0.en: "How long is it ago?": Of course Christ knew everything, but the purpose of the question is to make clear to the crowd, and teach them, that nothing is difficult for Him however long the time, or however long the cruelty and severity of the sickness.

9.12.1.en: And the father went on in his answer, explaining other things Satan had done to his son, for he tried to kill him many times, and often cast him into the fire and into the water to destroy him.

9.12.2.en: "If Thou canst": a question that reflects the man's hope that Christ was able to heal his son on the one hand, and in its tone also carries doubt of this ability on the other hand, or let us say weakness of faith. "Have compassion on us, and help us": that is, the son and the father, and on his mother and all his family.

9.13.0.en: "If Thou canst": Christ answered the man with the same words as he had asked, and the meaning is: I can do all things, but My work, and all My works, are seen only by the one who believes in this power of Mine; and your doubt and the weakness of your faith is the greatest obstacle to your son's healing.

9.14.0.en: "Cried out ... with tears": the man's answer came expressing his state. His crying out meant: I have no hope but You. And his tears express his weakness and his apology for his lack of trust. Then he declared his faith, and expressed that he was truly weak in faith, asking Christ's help in strengthening and completing his incomplete faith.

9.15.0.en: The crowd grew exceedingly, and Christ commanded Satan to come out by rebuking him, describing him as unclean - like all his kingdom - and called him: "Thou dumb and deaf spirit", to make clear that Satan is the cause of these two symptoms.

9.15.1.en: "I charge thee": this shows us the divinity of Christ and His absolute authority over the kingdom of darkness and its powers, and that none of it can resist Him or disobey Him. So He went on: "come out of him, and enter no more into him", that is, do not return to him again.

9.16.0.en: "And cried": the defeated and despairing Satan is the one crying out here, expressing his fury at coming out, and so he threw the boy to the ground, fainting and motionless, until many thought that he was dead. But Christ, in His tenderness, went up to the boy and took him by the hand ... and raised him, and he rose up with Him, healed of every sickness.

9.17.0.en: After the end of the event, when the disciples were alone with Christ, they asked Him the secret of their inability, and whether they had lost their authority over unclean spirits given to them in (Mt 10:1), or what? Christ's answer to them came: the gift given by God must be preserved by the spiritual life, represented in asking God's constant help "prayer", and in rising above the world and its desires and material things "fasting". So it is, my friend ... we see that faith is the essence of the relationship with God, and without it we lose the sight of His work in our lives. And sadly, currents of rationalism and doubt in God's ability to solve our problems have increased, and worry and anxiety have grown, while the problems remained as they were...

9.17.1.en: Do you not agree with me that both of us need to cry out in our prayer, saying: "Lord, I believe; help Thou mine unbelief"? And before we begin with our minds, is it not better to experience God's hand in helping us?

9.18.s.en: (4) The announcement of His death and a talk about greatness

9.18.0.en: As the Lord Christ did in the previous chapter (vv. 31-32), (and spoke of His being delivered up, His death and His resurrection, He repeats the same words here in preparing His disciples for the difficult events of the future.

9.19.0.en: "They understood not": not because of the difficulty of the saying itself, for the words are understandable linguistically, but because what the Lord Christ was saying was far from the picture in their imagination of His awaited kingdom with its earthly glory. "And were afraid": that is, they preferred not to ask Him, because of their embarrassment to speak about this matter ... and the truth is that not one of them understood any of Christ's declarations until after the redemption and the resurrection.

9.20.0.en: A conversation went on among the disciples as they walked. And when they arrived at the house (most likely Peter's house), the Lord Christ asked them what had been said among them. The purpose of His question was not to know - for He knows all things - but to teach the disciples and correct a mistaken notion in them, for they were occupied with the thought of who was the greatest among them, and its basis was pride of heart.

9.21.0.en: The Lord Christ sat down and gathered His disciples around Him, and began to teach at once: whoever wishes to be greater and lord of all must be a servant, putting himself last of all and less than everyone.

9.21.1.en: And what Christ teaches here completely contradicts the world's notion of greatness, for the world's greatness is domination, pride and control "... the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them" (Mt 20:25). But the greatness of Christianity is humility, denial of self and service of the other) ... see the explanation of Mt 20:20-28).

9.22.0.en: In tenderness, the Lord Christ took a child and embraced him, while still directing His words to His disciples, saying: whoever offers a work, however small - such as showing tenderness to a child in the name of Christ - Christ considers it a work offered to Himself personally and to the Father who sent Him; what matters is service and self-giving for the sake of others, and not the outward appearance of leadership or greatness.

9.23.s.en: (5) Service in the name of Christ

9.23.0.en: In (v. 37), the Lord said: "Whosoever shall receive ... in My name". Perhaps this saying made John remember an event he had gone through with the disciples, when they saw a man using the Lord's name to cast out devils, and he was not one of the Twelve nor one of the seventy apostles, so zeal seized them and they forbade him because he was not one of them.

9.24.0.en: The Lord reproved them for forbidding him, for the man was a believer and a lover of Christ, and his faith was the reason Satan went out ... whoever has experienced Me and experienced the power of My work with him will not turn against Me or blaspheme My name ... And as long as a man does not resist the truth and the sound faith delivered to the Church by Christ, there is no need to forbid him, otherwise it would become a desire to monopolize gifts and service.

9.25.0.en: So if the deed is small, even if someone gives you - in My name - a cup of water, he shall not lose his reward, how much more then the one who uses My name to have mercy on a sick person and cast a devil out of him?!

9.25.2.en: The Lord says in (v. 40): "He that is not against us is on our part", and in (Mt; 12:30, Lk 11:23):

9.25.3.en: "He that is not with Me is against Me". At first glance it may seem that the two meanings contradict each other, but in truth the meaning is one, because neutrality in the matter of faith in Christ is impossible; one is either with Him or against Him, with the actions that follow from that. To clarify we say:

9.25.4.en: The sign of friendship may be not resisting Christ, and so we understand: "He that is not against us - does not resist us - is on our part". And the sign of enmity may be not taking part in the positive work, so we understand: "He that is not with Me - in My work - is against Me".

9.26.0.en: The teaching here about not causing stumbling is a teaching for the disciples in general, for servants and for all believers, and it shows the seriousness of causing the simple in faith to stumble. And "he who causes to stumble" means the one who was a direct cause of another's error, or caused him confusion and doubts by unsound teaching, a wrong saying or a shameful act.

9.26.1.en: And because of the seriousness of this sin and its evil in God's sight, He says: it is better for a man that a millstone (a large stone for grinding grain) be hanged about his neck and he be cast into the sea, to die, than that he cause one who is simple in his faith to stumble.

9.27.0.en: The detailed explanation of this text was given before in (Mt 5:29-30, 18:8-9), and we shall be content here to clarify the following meanings:

9.27.1.en: "Cut it off ... pluck it out": cutting off the hand or the foot or plucking out the eye is not a literal meaning but a figurative meaning, intended that a man cut off all causes and ways of evil whose source is his senses or the people around him. The Lord Christ used the words "cutting off and plucking out" to show us the degree of decisiveness required of us all in facing stumbling blocks and their entrances, for a small stumbling block produces great evil.

9.27.2.en: "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched": another expression that terrifies the one who makes light of God's just recompense, and everyone who is careless about his senses and makes himself stumble, or becomes a cause of stumbling for others ... for the words "dieth not - is not quenched" are evidence of the eternity of the torment and that it does not cease.

9.27.3.en: So it is, my friend ... all who are deceived by the pleasures of the world and its temporal, passing desires drive themselves to a torment severe in its intensity, and the worse is that it never ends.

9.28.0.en: The talk in the preceding verses is about fleeing from sin and stumbling, and this is what the Fathers call negative striving. But the talk in this verse is about positive striving, and the intended meaning is: just as every sacrifice offered to God is salted with salt in order to preserve it, so the spiritual person must preserve himself, not only by fleeing and avoiding stumbling blocks, but also by growing in the virtues that preserve him and give him a savor before God, and these virtues are like fire in its light and in spreading warmth to others (Ex 43:24).

9.28.1.en: Take care, friend, of repentance and constant striving against all sources of stumbling, and flee for your life with all your strength, drawing others with you as far as possible...

9.29.0.en: But if virtue in the believer's life becomes without saltness, that is, without taste, and faded in color, then the man cannot be accepted by God. Therefore strive to live by virtue so that you may have salt in yourselves, that is, that each of you may have peace with himself, and all of you peace toward one another.

9.29.1.en: Beloved, give attention in the sacrament of repentance and confession, not only to recounting the obvious sins by which you grieved God's heart, but also declare your shortcoming in the Christian virtues, and ask your father for guidance and training, so that we may all be salted with a salt by which we please our Christ...

9.29.2.en: Hindrances to reaching God: divorce, love of money, leadership
